As of 2026-07-20, more than 210,000 people have been reached with prevention messages, though this is only a fraction of the millions at risk. CARE DRC reports funding cuts weakening health systems and the humanitarian response, while deploying over 500 community health workers for door-to-door outreach to educate communities and combat misinformation. Delivery of medical supplies faces rainfall-related delays through muddy, flooded routes; a recent Ituri shipment included new hospital beds to strengthen a CARE-supported facility. Complicating response is resistance from parts of local communities to strict hygiene and epidemiological measures, fueled by distrust and non-acceptance of some health recommendations. Health services continue to monitor the situation and implement measures to curb further transmission. The defendants are Mai Văn Quang (1973, Thanh Hóa) the alleged mastermind; Hà Văn Nghĩa (1978, Thanh Hóa) driver; Trần Thị Ngọc Hiền (Hoa Châu) (1964, Đông Hà); Hoàng Thị Mộng Truyền (Nương) (1972, Đông Hà); Trương Văn Quốc (1973, Đông Hà); and Trần Ngọc Bắc (1971, Đông Hà). An inter-provincial operation was uncovered by the Economic Police, with a May 19 interception of 172 pigs (9,968 kg) moved from a dedicated vehicle (plate 89A-874.XX) to smaller trucks near the Old Dong Ha Cemetery and the Quán Ngang Industrial Zone. Inspectors found no invoices or veter
- On July 19, 2026, Quảng Trị Provincial Police charged six suspects with violations of food safety regulations in a crackdown on an inter-provincial trafficking ring that bought, transported, and slaughtered pigs infected with African swine fever (ASF). The operation, described as a major investigative campaign, allegedly moved and processed more than 250 tons of diseased pigs across multiple provinces, creating a serious threat to consumer health from ASF-contaminated pork. The case demonstrates authorities' efforts to disrupt the illegal ASF pork supply chain and prevent unsafe meat from reaching markets. The charges were filed as part of ongoing enforcement against individuals involved in the inter-provincial trade and slaughter of diseased animals.
- Six people indicted in Quảng Trị Province, Vietnam, for importing African swine fever (ASF)–infected pigs from northern provinces, slaughtering them locally, and selling the meat. The case, announced on 19 July 2026, shows that from February to May 2026 the ring moved diseased pigs from trucks bearing Hung Yen license plates to Đông Hà's old cemetery area and the Quảng Ngang Industrial Zone, where the animals were slaughtered for profit. Mai Văn Quang and Hà Văn Nghĩa (both from Thanh Hóa) and Trần Thị Ngọc Hiền were arrested on charges of violating food safety regulations; Hoàng Thị Mộng Truyền, Trương Văn Quốc, and Trần Ngọc Bắc (all from Quảng Trị) were indicted and released on bail as the case expands. More than 250 tons of ASF-infected pigs were sold; the investigation continues.
- Quảng Trị authorities busted a cross-provincial trafficking ring that imported over 250 tons of pigs diseased with African swine fever (ASF) from northern provinces to the Tây Trì slaughterhouse in Quảng Trị for slaughter and sale, February–May 2026. On 19 July 2026, the provincial police indicted six suspects for violations of food safety regulations. The operation, aimed at profiting from ASF-contaminated meat, underscores a significant risk to consumer health and highlights gaps in meat safety enforcement across provinces. No human cases are reported; the outbreak concern centers on animal disease control and meat safety within the supply chain, with investigations focusing on the source of infected livestock and the handling of imported/transported animals.
- Six defendants in Quảng Trị Province were indicted for violating food safety regulations in a large-scale scheme to buy, transport, slaughter, and market pigs infected with African swine fever (ASF). Authorities say more than 250 tons of diseased pigs were moved to Quảng Trị for slaughter and sale. On 19 May, police intercepted pigs transferred from a dedicated truck to a smaller vehicle near Đông Hà’s old public cemetery and the Quán Ngang industrial area. Inspection found 172 pigs weighing about 9,968 kg, with two dead; no origin papers or veterinary certificates. Laboratory tests confirmed ASF in 18 pigs. Investigations traced purchases from February–May 2026 in northern provinces (Bắc Ninh, Hưng Yên), then transport to Quảng Trị, slaughter at Tây Trì slaughterhouse, and market release.

article.articleHeadline: The trajectory of the COVID-19 pandemic is now clear; seniors over 60 should be aware of these few things.
article.articleSummary:
- COVID-19 persists in China as a seasonal respiratory illness, not vanished. Since Oct 2025, national surveillance shows low overall activity with seasonal fluctuations; the NB.1.8.1 variant mainly causes upper respiratory infections with little lung injury in healthy individuals. Severe disease remains concentrated in people aged 60 and older, especially with chronic conditions. The trajectory is threefold: ongoing mutation without major virulence increases, seasonal influenza-like transmission, and high risk among the elderly. - COVID-19 is resurging in China this summer. In June, nationwide new confirmed infections reached about 79,000, with outpatient/ED positivity rising from 2.9% to 6.4%. The dominant Omicron NB.1.8.1 sub-lineage continues to drive immune escape. Despite a seasonal rebound, the public health impact remains moderate: June severe cases were 130 and deaths 1, with overall risk lower than in 2024. Summer transmission is fueled by waning immunity, ongoing travel, and crowded indoor spaces with air conditioning that dry the mucosa. Preventive guidance emphasizes six household essentials: 1) surgical or N95 masks; 2) symptom-relief antiviral/antipyretics; 3) home pulse oximeter; 4) disinfectants (75% alcohol, wipes, hand sanitizer); 5) throat lozenges and saline nasal spray; 6) portable thermometer.

article.articleHeadline: Djugu: Alarming rise in suspected community deaths amid the Ebola response - ACP
article.articleSummary: Suspected Ebola outbreaks in Héritage health area, Walendu Djatsi sector, Djugu district, Ituri Province, northeastern DRC, with over 200 burials reported amid an alarming rise in community deaths. Nine health posts have already closed, with three more at risk. Authorities link the spread to a pregnant woman exhibiting Ebola symptoms who was admitted to a health facility lacking adequate protection, then traveled through multiple posts, exposing many people. In response, authorities announced intensified surveillance in villages and strict controls on corpse repatriation to curb transmission. Village chiefs were instructed to enforce precautions and to sanction any unauthorized body transfers. Community leaders were urged to cooperate with response teams, especially during funerals, to interrupt transmission chains. The Héritage area, comprising 12 health posts, is facing major disruptions to routine health services and requires rapid infection-control actions to prevent a larger outbreak.

Include citrus fruits—lemon, orange, mosambi (sweet lime), and chakotra (grapefruit)—and consider a morning lemon water or a daily orange. Amla (Indian gooseberry) is described as a superfood with about 20 times more Vitamin C than other sour fruits and aids detoxification. Together, these foods may bolster immunity and digestion during the monsoon.

article.articleHeadline: Stomach infection or food poisoning? Don't skip lab tests this monsoon | Mint
article.articleSummary: Monsoon conditions drive a surge in stomach infections and food poisoning, fueled by contaminated water, rapid food spoilage in hot, humid weather, street-food exposure to rain and flies, and poor hygiene. Food poisoning results from toxins produced by bacteria in spoiled food; symptoms typically appear within hours and resolve with rest and fluids. By contrast, stomach infections involve live bacteria, viruses, or parasites multiplying in the gut, often linked to contaminated water during flooding and waterlogging; these infections can linger, worsen, and cause dehydration, with possible complications such as typhoid or hepatitis A. Lab tests are essential to distinguish the two and guide treatment. Dr LakshmiPriya R of Chennai (Metropolis Healthcare) and Dr Anukalp Prakash of CK Birla Gurgaon caution that monsoon-specific exposure raises risk; prompt diagnosis and lab confirmation.

article.articleHeadline: Chandipura Virus Knocks: Six-Year-Old Girl from Dungarpur Dies in the Village
article.articleSummary: In Rajasthan’s Dungarpur district, a six-year-old girl from Ratanpura village (Simlavada area) died after a suspected Chandipura Virus (CHPV) infection, with treatment in Gujarat’s Himmatnagar hospital; death occurred on 15 July 2026. CHPV confirmation is not yet established; samples were sent for testing and authorities await lab results. Gujarat notified Rajasthan; on 18 July, Rajasthan’s health department directed Dungarpur administration to tighten precautionary measures. Health teams have been deployed in the village, with 353 people screened to date. CHPV is carried primarily by sand flies and can also involve mosquitoes and ticks; it mainly affects children under 15 and presents with fever, vomiting and flu-like symptoms, with the possibility of encephalitis in severe cases. Officials urge medical consultation if symptoms appear.

She has started free antiretroviral therapy at a government hospital. This case highlights the risk of HIV transmission through non-sterile tattoo equipment and the need for strict infection-control practices in parlours. No information on Hepatitis B result or additional cases is provided.

article.articleHeadline: E. coli found in Bengal's puchka water as stomach infection cases rise
article.articleSummary: Escherichia coli detected in flavoured puchka water from roadside vendors in Khanakul-Arambagh, Hooghly district, West Bengal, linked to rising stomach ache, vomiting and diarrhoea among residents. Laboratory tests confirmed E. coli in samples collected from four vendors. Health officials warn contamination could trigger severe gastrointestinal infections and, in some cases, respiratory and urinary tract infections. Block Medical Officer of Health Dr Ratim Chatterjee urges use of sealed packaged drinking water for puchka preparation, improved hygiene, handwashing after handling money, clean utensils, and keeping potato filling and flavoured water covered. Some strains can produce toxins causing cramps, bloody diarrhoea and kidney failure, says Dr Pradeep Das of the IMA. Authorities are inspecting vendors; licensing under the Food Safety and Quality Control Department is being considered. The IMA has launched an awareness campaign, advising particularly children and elderly people to avoid roadside foods.

article.articleHeadline: Mandsaur Girls' Hostel Food Poisoning News: Several girls fell ill one after another, rushed to hospital; doctors revealed a shocking reason after investigation.
article.articleSummary: Mandsaur, Madhya Pradesh: In Garoth, at the Girls’ Hostel run by the Department of Tribal Welfare, several students fell ill on Sunday with vomiting, diarrhea and abdominal pain, prompting hospitalisation at a government facility. Doctors reported dehydration and symptoms consistent with food poisoning; the exact cause will be known only after laboratory confirmation. The hostel superintendent denied that the meals were contaminated, noting that all 35 residents reportedly ate the same food on Saturday night, though some had outside drinking water. Authorities moved quickly: a Naib Tehsildar visited the hospital, and Joint Commissioner Anuradha from Ujjain ordered a departmental inquiry; a food inspector is investigating. After treatment, the students were discharged in stable condition. No deaths reported; investigation ongoing to identify the infection source, whether food-related or otherwise.

article.articleHeadline: Interview | African Swine Fever Vaccine To Hit Market in Six Months: Veterinarian
article.articleSummary: India's first indigenous African Swine Fever (ASF) vaccine is set to hit the market in six months, after successful trials at the Government Pig Breeding Farm in Ambikapur and a launch announced by Union Agriculture Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan. ASF is a viral disease of pigs with 100% mortality, causing massive losses since its arrival in India in 2020, first affecting the Northeastern states and Punjab. Vaccine development used virus antigen from Punjab and the Northeast, coordinated by the High Security Animal Disease Laboratory in Bhopal (an ICAR Delhi facility) after four to five years of research. Trials at Ambikapur began in March, involving 50 pigs across ages (piglets, young, adults, pregnant sows). The team visited Ambikapur every 15 days; at Sakalo farm they collected blood, serum, and nasal samples, which were sent to Bhopal for laboratory testing.

article.articleHeadline: Is your pack of instant noodles safe? Health experts share what to check in the wake of recent food poisoning cases
article.articleSummary: As of 19 July 2026, two consumer court cases in India linked expired instant noodles to severe food poisoning. In Kangra, Himachal Pradesh, a father’s purchase of Spicy Korean noodles led to severe illness in his minor daughter; wrapper showed expiry nearly three months earlier, and the Kangra District Consumer Commission fined the retailer ₹20,000 for selling expired inventory. In Kurnool district, Andhra Pradesh, a man buying two packets developed high fever, stomach pain, and vomiting; the packets were expired, and the consumer court ordered a ₹2.8 lakh penalty against the retailer. The incidents underscore checking expiration dates and proper storage. Guidance includes storing noodles in a cool, dry place and preparing them per manufacturer instructions using safe drinking water.

article.articleHeadline: Stay Vigilant As COVID Cases Rise in Neighbouring States: Doctors
article.articleSummary: Covid-19 cases are rising in neighbouring states, but Hyderabad doctors urge no panic; the illness is seasonal and present year-round, often alongside other infections. Elderly, children, pregnant women, and people with non-communicable diseases (diabetes, cancer, asthma) or on long-term steroids should take precautions and avoid self-medication or buying OTC drugs without a clinician. Health authorities are monitoring cases, issuing guidelines to primary health centers, basti dawakhanas, and tertiary hospitals, with rapid-response teams visiting areas reporting symptoms. Travellers from neighbouring states have shown symptoms and should isolate; one Tirupati family experienced high fever, loss of taste, and extreme fatigue, taking about 10 days to recover. Covid-19 testing is not routinely recommended unless illness is severe or involves the lungs, with treatment guided by symptoms and isolation for affected family members.

article.articleHeadline: 45 bitten by suspected rabid dog as it runs through Madurai
article.articleSummary: In Madurai, Tamil Nadu, a suspected rabid stray dog bit 45 people as it ran from Arapalayam toward the Meenakshi Sundareswarar Temple on Saturday, triggering panic in temple precincts. One victim, Gajendran, said the dog first attacked a child near a tea shop in Jaihindpuram and then bit him on the leg when it returned. Madurai Corporation deployed dog-catching teams to capture the animal, administer anti-rabies vaccine, and relocate it to a shelter. All 45 victims received anti-rabies vaccination at urban primary health centres or Government Rajaji Hospital. The incident follows rising stray-dog aggression in areas such as Villapuram, Anuppanadi, MK Puram and Solai Alagupuram. Madurai registered about 19,000 dog bite/scratch cases in 2025, with 15–25 incidents daily. Vaccination will be intensified over five months, with four vehicles vaccinating around 300 dogs daily; about 40,000 strays exist, 22,000 vaccinated so far, six-day drives. An NGO-assisted drive vaccinated 268 dogs across Narimedu, BB Kulam, Madakulam and Pasumalai on Saturday; sterilisation runs accompany vaccination.

article.articleHeadline: As Covid cases rise, AP doctor's delta-wave study offers lessons
article.articleSummary: As of 19 July 2026, amid a fresh uptick in Covid-19 cases in Andhra Pradesh, a home-based treatment protocol developed by Dr. Yanamadala Muralikrishna (Kakinada) significantly reduced hospitalisations among mild Covid-19 from 13.3% to 1.7%, per a May–Aug 2026 Journal of Primary Care Specialties study. In Lakshmi Vaidyasala, Kakinada, 120 patients were randomized: 60 received the standard state kit (Doxycycline, Ivermectin, Paracetamol); 60 received the specialized regimen (Aspirin, Prednisolone, Azithromycin) targeting excessive inflammation, hypercoagulability and secondary bacterial infection. Outcomes favored the specialized protocol: 1/60 hospitalised vs 8/60; faster recovery and fewer long-Covid symptoms such as fatigue and dry cough. The protocol, first shared in April 2021 during the Delta-wave crisis with oxygen shortages, emphasizes early diagnosis, medical supervision and timely evidence-based treatment to ease hospital pressure and improve patient outcomes in ongoing outbreaks.

Residents Sanjay Kumar and Rajendra P Joshi claim that a contractor abandoned work nearly 24 months after GMC takeover, worsening conditions and traffic jams. Many believe the Ghaziabad Development Authority (GDA) would have addressed tasks more effectively. Community groups urge RWAs and citizens to unite and escalate complaints through official channels if not resolved. GMC officials counter that they are actively addressing complaints. The piece highlights fear of dengue- and malaria-related outbreaks linked to stagnant water, but provides no confirmed cases, laboratory results, or infection sources beyond the alleged stagnation and drainage issues.

article.articleHeadline: The threat of climate change is no longer just about the weather; the risk of tuberculosis is also increasing.
article.articleSummary: Indonesia faces growing health risks from climate change, with tuberculosis (TB) control among those affected. The CARES program, Climate Action for Resilient and Empowered Healthcare Staff, developed by KUMPUL Impact with AVPN support, strengthens health workers and community cadres to address climate-TB intersections. The initiative kicked off on 21 October 2025, bringing academics, health practitioners, civil society, and communities to explore links between climate and health-system resilience. Prof. Budi Haryanto of University of Indonesia notes climate impacts on health are evident and may rise, potentially increasing TB risks and worsening non-communicable diseases, food security, mental health, and socioeconomic conditions. TB patients may face interrupted treatment and higher household costs during climate events. CARES developed Climate-TB training modules and delivered webinars via Plataran Sehat, with cadre training alongside PPTI Pusat, covering vulnerable groups, transmission, and health-service access challenges. Policy integration, research gaps, and cross-sector collaboration remain priorities.

article.articleHeadline: HIV cases exceed 10,000; Papua Highlands population facing a sharp decline
article.articleSummary: HIV/AIDS in Papua Highlands has reached 10,104 reported cases across eight districts, signaling ongoing transmission and rising public health burden. Active prevention and response efforts are evident in Jayawijaya, Mamberamo Tengah, and Tolikara, with commendations from Yomi Kogoya, head of the Papua Highlands AIDS Control Commission (KPA). He urges broader collaboration with civil society groups and working groups to strengthen education, prevention, and patient support, calling on KPA offices in the remaining five districts to resume or intensify programs. Notably, he emphasizes dedication over funding, stating staff should stay active even without budget support. The report provides no details on infection sources or laboratory confirmation. Warnings highlight potential severe impacts on the indigenous Papua population if HIV/AIDS is not addressed, projecting adverse effects over the next 10–15 years. Published 2026-07-19.

article.articleHeadline: Chickenpox Drama, From the Community Health Center to the Emergency Department
article.articleSummary: As of 19 July 2026, an Indonesian case of chickenpox (varicella) caused by Varicella zoster virus is described. During the post-holiday period, the patient developed nocturnal low-grade fever and fatigue before two fluid-filled vesicles appeared on the upper arm and a generalized, intensely itchy vesicular rash spread across the body. Although chickenpox is typically self-limiting, the account notes the possibility of reinfection, albeit rare, due to a mild primary illness, infection in infancy, or waning immunity. Care was sought at a community health clinic (Puskesmas) where examination confirmed varicella. Treatment consisted of acyclovir tablets (five times daily for a total of ten pills per day), ibuprofen for pain, a daily vitamin, and topical acyclovir. The piece underscores high contagion and primary-care management in Indonesia.

article.articleHeadline: Strengthen the Integration of Medical Services, East Kalimantan Reduces Dengue Fever Death Toll
article.articleSummary: East Kalimantan authorities strengthen integrated medical services to curb dengue fever (Demam Berdarah Dengue, DBD) fatalities. Dinas Kesehatan (Dinkes) East Kalimantan, led by Jaya Mualimin, states case reviews go beyond administrative records, using lessons to raise service quality after recent DBD deaths in Samarinda and Paser. An in-depth evaluation engages DBD program managers, public health centers (puskesmas), and hospitals to pinpoint precise improvements and ensure seamless care. Key focus is early detection and rapid, accurate patient management, with solid coordination across facilities from primary care to referral hospitals. The strategy aims to protect residents by unifying care pathways and communications. Current data show 1,530 dengue infections in East Kalimantan, with two fatalities in Mahakam Ulu and Kota Bontang, reflecting improved fatality control through integrated services.

article.articleHeadline: Bio-TCV Vaccine, Part of the Effort to Prevent Infectious Diseases - Suara Merdeka Jakarta
article.articleSummary: Bio-TCV, a typhoid conjugate vaccine from Bio Farma, is part of Indonesia’s effort to strengthen infectious disease prevention, linking vaccination with sanitation, clean water, and safe food to combat typhoid fever caused by Salmonella Typhi. Domestic production aims to ensure a sustainable supply and broaden National Immunization Program coverage across Indonesia. Regulatory and clinical milestones include BPOM registration on 20 August 2023 after Phase III trials involving 3,071 participants aged 6 months to 60 years. PAPDI’s Adult Immunization Task Force chair Dr. Sukamto Koesnoe recommends vaccinating adults 18+, especially high-risk groups, citing favorable safety, immunogenicity, and potential longer protection. Implementation emphasizes affordable pricing, collaboration with health professionals, and education to embed vaccination within an integrated preventive approach alongside improved sanitation and access to clean water.

article.articleHeadline: Hansen's Disease Is Curable: Recognize Its Symptoms and How It Is Transmitted Early.
article.articleSummary: Hansen's disease (leprosy), caused by Mycobacterium leprae, remains a public health concern in Manado, Indonesia. The infection is curable when detected and treated early, though it is infectious and not as easily transmitted as commonly perceived. Dr. Reymond Sondakh, Sp.DVE, of Perdoski Manado, explains that leprosy primarily affects skin and peripheral nerves, but can involve the eyes and upper respiratory tract. Early signs include skin patches that are lighter, redder, or darker and fail to heal, often with loss of sensation or numbness. Tingling or numbness may occur in hands and feet, with nerve enlargement at the elbows, wrists, behind the knees, or in the neck, sometimes accompanied by pain. Advanced cases may have non-painful wounds on hands or feet and facial changes, such as difficulty closing the eyes and thinning eyebrows. Emphasis on early recognition to enable timely treatment and prevent disability. (July 19, 2026, Manado)

article.articleHeadline: Parasites on raw vegetables: how to eat safely?
article.articleSummary: Cyclosporiasis, a diarrheal illness caused by Cyclospora cayetanensis, is linked to raw vegetables. The US CDC reports thousands of cases across many states, with hundreds linked to a single contaminated source; leafy greens are under surveillance. Cyclospora contaminates produce via irrigation water, soil, harvest, or handling, causing watery diarrhea, abdominal pain, bloating, nausea, fatigue, and weight loss; fever is usually mild. Children, the elderly, and immunocompromised individuals face higher dehydration and hospitalization risk. In Vietnam, where many dishes include raw herbs, washing under running water (sometimes with vinegar) is advised, though not foolproof; heating to 72°C or higher reduces risk. No confirmed cyclosporiasis cases in Vietnam yet, but precautions are advised. Separately, in Gia Lai province, dozens developed abdominal pain and diarrhea after eating bread at a shop on Hung Vuong Street, Quy Nhơn Ward, and were hospitalized.

article.articleHeadline: Three suspected cases of pulmonary tuberculosis due to cigarette smoking were identified.

Screening in Mai Phụ, Lộc Hà, and Hồng Lộc communes enrolled 902 residents who underwent chest X-rays; 811 were tested for latent TB infection, with 15 positives, and 270 were tested for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, revealing three pulmonary TB cases. All three patients had long-term histories of cigarette smoking. The initiative also flagged 351 individuals with symptoms suggestive of asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, prompting spirometry for lung function monitoring. Health authorities emphasize that tobacco use increases TB risk and worsens treatment outcomes. The program’s emphasis on community-based, high-risk screening aims to enable early TB diagnosis, curb transmission, and strengthen provincial TB control efforts.

article.articleHeadline: Rescuing a woman in septic shock due to a ruptured splenic abscess
article.articleSummary: Seventy-year-old woman with septic shock due to a ruptured splenic abscess, accompanied by respiratory failure and multi-organ failure, was successfully treated at Gia An 115 Hospital in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam. The case highlights the decisive role of rapid, multidisciplinary collaboration and timely surgical intervention in severe infectious diseases. Coordinated action across specialties enabled definitive management of the ruptured splenic abscess and comprehensive organ support, leading to stabilization and recovery. The report underscores how early recognition and prompt surgical care can alter outcomes in life-threatening intra-abdominal infections. Location: Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam; hospital: Gia An 115 Hospital. Published 2026-07-19.

article.articleHeadline: Nollowa Chicken Thụy Khuê accused of food poisoning after a customer was hospitalized.
article.articleSummary: Two customers ordered takeout from Nollowa Chicken, Thụy Khuê, Hanoi, on July 15. A social-media post by a Hanoi resident alleges that after eating the fried chicken, one person experienced abdominal pain and vomiting and was hospitalized with a gastrointestinal infection, while the other diner remained asymptomatic. The restaurant confirmed the incident, noting the meal was shared by two people and only one developed symptoms. They conducted internal checks: chicken is delivered fresh daily and cooked after order; frying oil kept at about 180°C with 15–20 minutes frying per their routine; ingredients’ expiry dates were reviewed with no abnormalities found, and no further complaints have been reported to date. The cause remains undetermined; while factors such as individual susceptibility or interactions with other foods are possible, no medical conclusion has been made. The customer has not contacted the restaurant, though the post circulated online and public interest continues.

article.articleHeadline: A Decade of Cutting-Edge Refinement: Taiwan's Enterovirus Vaccine Breaks onto the International Stage
article.articleSummary: At BIO Asia-Taiwan 2026, Taiwan's High-End Vaccines (6547) presented ENVACGEN, an Enterovirus 71 (EV71) vaccine, targeting the 2–6 month infant window. The company extended dosing to 56 days to boost antibody response, differentiating from competitors. A self-built GMP facility costing nearly NT$4 billion supports consistent Phase 3 trials and scalable production. In Phase 3 across Taiwan, Vietnam and other centers, the vaccine achieved zero breakthrough infections with an efficacy estimate of 100% (approximately 96.8% CI), with results published in The Lancet. Regulatory navigation remains a major hurdle, prompting partnerships with local pediatric distributors. In Taiwan, ENVACGEN already holds >90% market share; Vietnam granted the first EV71 vaccine license in 2026, with Singapore and other ASEAN markets slated for expansion, signaling a broader international push for Taiwan’s biotech sector.

article.articleSummary: China reports rising COVID-19 numbers again: June infections about 79,000, with 130 severe cases and one death; all June samples were Omicron NB.1.8.1 and its sublines. In the 27th week of 2026, surveillance lists influenza at 11.6%, SARS-CoV-2 at 9.6%, and enteroviruses at 9.1% as leading respiratory pathogens. Experts warn of new Omicron subvariants and question the reliability of Beijing’s official data, sparking online debate over mortality counts. Taiwan registered 2,811 new cases in the week to July 6, including 17 severe cases and no deaths. Dr. Feng cautions about PQ.16.1.1, a highly mutated Omicron descendant of NB.1.8.1, spreading across the mainland and Southeast Asia; reinfections in previously infected individuals may be more severe, though initial infections show mortality below 1%. Genomic surveillance also notes other strains such as RF.5.

Hamid, clinical researcher Syed Manwar Ali, Federal Health Secretary Aslam Ghori, and DRAP CEO Dr. Ubaid. Estimates indicate over 1 million Pakistanis may be HDV-infected. The agreement is framed as a milestone for local access, bolstering domestic pharmaceutical capacity and international collaboration. DRAP is prioritizing regulatory approvals to accelerate availability. Phase II clinical trials reportedly show positive safety and efficacy results, signaling promising progress toward treating HDV in the country.

article.articleHeadline: Health campaign spotlights hepatitis B prevention across all ages
article.articleSummary: China's hepatitis B control campaign in Beijing aims to meet the 2030 goal to eliminate viral hepatitis as a public health threat. Some 75 million people aged 1–69 live with chronic HBV in the country, ~one-third of global cases, with many unaware of their status. Infant vaccination since 2005 has reached 99.6% coverage for the three-dose series and 95.6% for the timely birth dose, reducing hepatitis B surface antigen prevalence among children under five to 0.30%, while prevalence in 1–69-year-olds stands at 5.86%. A September 2025 action plan for 2025–2030 coordinates vaccination remaining high in infancy and expanding adult immunization. Experts Yao Fengli (PLA General Hospital) warns newborns have ~90% risk of chronic infection if infected at birth, underscoring prompt birth dose and 1-, 6-month boosters. Lyv Sa notes non-transmission via everyday contact; Zhang Ying highlights grassroots centers in Beijing and Tianjin for education, screening, follow-up.

article.articleHeadline: Find out the symptoms of West Nile virus after the first case was detected in Tel Aviv | Masrawy
article.articleSummary: First confirmed West Nile virus case detected in Tel Aviv, Israel, amid mosquito season. West Nile virus is primarily transmitted to humans by bites from infected mosquitoes feeding on birds, the natural reservoir; humans and horses can be infected but do not spread it. The virus circulates across Africa, Europe, the Middle East, North America, and West Asia. It was first identified in 1937 in the West Nile region of Uganda; a virulent lineage emerged in 1997 in Israel, with the 1999 US introduction triggering a major outbreak. About 80% of infections are asymptomatic; ~20% develop West Nile fever with fever, headache, fatigue, muscle and body pains, nausea or vomiting, and sometimes a trunk rash. Rare cases progress to neuroinvasive disease (meningitis, encephalitis) with severe headache, neck stiffness, altered consciousness, tremors, seizures, or paralysis. Incubation 3–14 days; diagnosis via antibody or viral RNA tests. No approved human vaccine; treatment is supportive.

article.articleHeadline: Frontline Observations on Disaster Prevention, Mitigation, and Relief | A Day in the Life of Local CDC Personnel in Disaster Areas
article.articleSummary: Flood-response operations in Guangxi’s Hengzhou (a district under Nanning City) mobilized over 500 personnel from the Nanning CDC to three flood-affected areas: Hengzhou, Yunbiao Town, and Bin Yang Gantang, to conduct post-disaster sanitation and disease prevention. On July 18, teams moved by foot along mud-laden roads to Dengxu Village and Wangbaotun, delivering disinfection spray and health education to about 140 households. They emphasized simple, correct mixing of chlorine disinfectants (one cap concentrate to one cap water) and wearing gloves and masks due to irritant disinfectants. Health education extended to village cadres to multiply reach. Officials warned that 7–15 days after flooding is a high-risk window for intestinal, respiratory, and vector-borne diseases; in addition to spraying, authorities will conduct mosquito/larval control and follow-up sanitation until all affected households are covered, then return to Nanning.

article.articleHeadline: Malaria had almost disappeared from this region; why is it coming back in force today?
article.articleSummary: Malaria resurges in Altamira, Brazilian Amazon, after a successful reduction tied to the Belo Monte hydroelectric dam. From 1,200 cases in 2013, annual cases dropped to about 60 by the project’s end, but have since climbed to more than 700 cases each year, chiefly in rural communities at the forest edge. A GeoHealth study analyzing more than 15 years of surveillance data and satellite forest-cover imagery linked the comeback to habitat changes from deforestation and hydroelectric development, but notes that stopping preventive measures after the project closed also fueled transmission. During construction, malaria control included indoor insecticide spraying, bed nets, and rapid diagnosis and treatment; these ended with the project. Since 2020, urban areas remain comparatively protected, while people living near the forest edge face highest risk. Brazil’s 2035 elimination goal requires sustained, targeted investment in high-risk zones, not early halting of measures.

article.articleHeadline: Winter increases canine influenza cases; learn how to prevent.
article.articleSummary: Winter-driven rise in canine influenza (canine infectious tracheobronchitis) cases is reported in the interior of São Paulo, Brazil, with emphasis on prevention and early diagnosis. A Brazilian Journal of Microbiology study found respiratory agents in 78% of dogs in communal settings (daycares, hotels, pet spaces) and 44% of positives showed coinfection. The disease can be caused by various viruses and bacteria, including Bordetella bronchiseptica. Although most cases improve with proper treatment, it can progress to serious respiratory infections in puppies, elderly dogs, and immunocompromised animals. Common symptoms include persistent dry cough, gagging, sneezing, nasal discharge, fatigue, fever, and reduced appetite; early veterinary care reduces severity and transmission. High-risk groups include brachycephalic breeds (Pug, French Bulldog, Shih Tzu, Boston Terrier). Prevention centers on vaccination plus hygiene and management measures to reduce spread in crowded dog facilities.

article.articleHeadline: The SUS system cross-references data from pharmacies and anticipates outbreaks.
article.articleSummary: Brazil's Ministry of Health is piloting ÆSOP, an Early Alert System for Outbreaks with Pandemic Potential, to detect nascent transmission by cross-referencing data from the SUS Primary Health Care network and over-the-counter medication sales (MIPs). The study, by Fiocruz Bahia researchers and Coppe/UFRJ, published in npj Digital Public Health, shows that pharmacy sales data signaled outbreaks before hospitalization rises in about 57% of 746 respiratory-illness episodes, while primary care data did so in about 60%. Signals appeared 1–3 weeks before increases in severe cases, enabling faster epidemiological investigations, expanded sampling, and hospital planning (beds, staff, supplies). The approach relies on syndromic surveillance (febrile, respiratory, diarrheal syndromes) via Sisab and IQVIA data, complementing lab-based confirmation. Regional differences exist; across roughly three-quarters of Brazil, at least one data source performed well. Historical examples include Ebola outbreaks in West Africa, Zika in Brazil, and SARS-CoV-2 in China to illustrate early detection.

article.articleHeadline: Drones Take Action Against Dengue and Reveal Critical Hotspots in São Carlos; Watch the Video.
article.articleSummary: On Friday, July 17, 2026, São Carlos, São Paulo, Brazil, deployed drones in six areas to combat Aedes aegypti, vector for dengue, chikungunya, Zika, and yellow fever. The operation covered 43 risk points across neighborhoods including Eduardo Abdelnur, Ipê Mirim, Zavaglia, Antenor Garcia, Cidade Aracy, Presidente Collor, Residencial Vida Nova São Carlos, Jardins Monte Carlo, Madre Cabrini, Gonzaga, parts of Pacaembu and Cruzeiro do Sul. Most hotspots were pools and open water tanks lacking proper coverage. Drones enable rapid detection and treatment, including dropping solid chlorine tablets into open water and accessory sites. Health officials stress technology complements vector-control visits and community effort. As of 2026, São Carlos reported 393 confirmed dengue cases with no deaths; 165 chikungunya and 154 Zika cases discarded; yellow fever had no notifications.

article.articleHeadline: El Niño increases the risk of epidemics and the spread of superbugs, expert warns.
article.articleSummary: El Niño increases epidemic risk and spread of resistant bacteria as of July 19, 2026. In Brazil, effects vary by region; in the South region, heavy rainfall heightens floods, landslides, and related health impacts. PAHO urges strengthened epidemiological surveillance and health-system operational capacity to maintain care during extreme weather. According to Viviane Hessel, leptospirosis, hepatitis A, and gastroenteritis are concerns as families seek shelter and face limited access to potable water, food, medications, and services; crowded settings may boost transmission of respiratory infections. Temperature increases may facilitate spread of antibiotic-resistance genes in the community and hospitals. A May 2026 Lancet Planetary Health study identified a global 10% rise in antibiotic-resistance genes, derived from analyses of more than 480,000 Salmonella genomes in 139 countries from 1940–2023. Preventive measures include hand hygiene, proper cleaning/disinfection, and strict infection-control protocols to reduce hospital transmission.

article.articleSummary: Rio Grande do Sul confirms a new avian influenza focus in backyard poultry in Coqueiros do Sul, RS. The suspicion was notified on July 15, and diagnosis was confirmed by the Federal Laboratory for Agricultural Defense in Campinas (LFDA-SP) after samples collected by the State Agriculture Secretariat. The finding does not affect the sanitary status of Brazilian commercial poultry or export prospects for chicken meat and eggs. A 10-kilometer surveillance radius will be established, with farm visits and guidance to producers to reinforce biosafety and early notification. Avian influenza is a contagious viral disease of birds; in rare cases it can infect mammals. Symptoms include apathy, reduced appetite, respiratory signs, facial/leg swelling, ataxia, torticollis, and mass mortality. Sick or dead birds should not be handled. Report suspicious signs to the State Veterinary Defense offices or WhatsApp (51) 98445-2033. RS has previously recorded cases in commercial, backyard, and wild birds.

article.articleHeadline: Fresh mosquito warning for anyone travelling to 7 regions
article.articleSummary: Fresh mosquito warning for travellers to seven regions: Southeast Asia, South Asia, Sub-Saharan Africa, Central and South America, the Caribbean, and Pacific islands. Dengue imported to England: 137 cases Jan–Jun 2026; 27 linked to travel to Thailand, 19 to the Maldives; end-June last year was 161. Chikungunya: 59 cases Jan–Jun 2026, Sri Lanka accounting for 18; 73 in the same period last year. Zika remains a concern, especially for pregnant women due to risk of stillbirth, miscarriage and developmental problems. Malaria: 557 cases in England, Wales and Northern Ireland Jan–May 2026; 548 at the same point last year. Typhoid and paratyphoid: 287 cases Jan–Jun 2026; Salmonella spread via contaminated food/water. Mosquitoes breed in standing water; eggs hatch when warm. Advice: TravelHealthPro for vaccination and meds; use repellents with DEET, icardin/picaridin or PMD; sleep under treated nets; maintain food/water hygiene; pregnant travelers should consult a clinician.

article.articleHeadline: Zambia Launches Third Polio Vaccination Campaign - ZNBC
article.articleSummary: Zambia launched the third round of the Oral Polio Vaccination Campaign in Lusaka, targeting children under five in six high-risk provinces, with WHO and UNICEF support. The drive follows the detection of a Type 2 poliovirus variant via environmental surveillance earlier this year; no confirmed paralysis cases have been reported. The government also unveiled a US$500,000 solar power system at the National Vaccine Store and handed over a refrigerated vaccine distribution truck to strengthen cold-chain storage and vaccine delivery. Africa CDC urged innovations to improve distribution, noting about 80% of vaccines require cold storage. Separately, the ministry reports ongoing measles transmission, with 39 new cases in 24 hours across five districts, bringing cumulative confirmed cases to 1,014 and 59 current hospitalizations.
